F2-field-6 (Which conditions does `ready` check, and how does an improver's skipped status affect downstream eligibility?) was settled by gemini: limitation. Section 4 already shows how skipping `verify` lets `draft` write the affected claims as hypotheses, and how any edit creates a new revision on which every gate must hold again. The generated description of galley does not list the individual gates, so listing the readiness predicates would invent details absent from the source material. The referee is right that Section 4 still omits this limitation. The edits state plainly in Section 4 and Section 8 that the generated description omits the individual gates and their predicates, while noting that no gate depends on a verification result or, in autonomous mode, waits for the sign-off sheet.

F2-editor-1 (What enforces scope fallback in the prose produced by the required drafting step?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right, and both seats agree on the underlying mechanics. The author's revisions in S3 already separate claim standing, drafting instructions, and code enforcement, and explain how the sign-off sheet records skipped post-draft checks. However, the single-section author responses could not edit the remaining sections, and frame wrote the abstract before review rather than after it. Consequently, the abstract, S4, S5, and S7 still phrase drafting instructions as guaranteed prose outputs or omit the role of the sign-off sheet when a post-draft check is skipped. The edits carry the distinction between claim standing, drafting instructions, code-enforced citation checks, unguaranteed post-draft model review, and sign-off for skipped checks across the abstract, S4, S5, and S7.

Final profile: input_not_output 2/3, shared_bottleneck 2/3, conventional_body_one_graft 1/3, surprising_and_certain 0/3, opens_more_than_closes 2/3, cheap_to_adopt 1/3, early 1/3. Weakest: surprising_and_certain. Compared with the pre-draft profile (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1), the finished manuscript retains the exact same score vector (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1). Reframing around scope-elastic compilation (Section 3; C34–C40) and maintaining scrupulous candour about enforcement boundaries and limitations (Sections 3, 5, 7, 8) produced an honest, coherent architectural account, an open-source package, and crisp follow-up designs (Section 9). However, honesty about missing evidence does not substitute for evidence: because the sole evaluation is a provisional, self-referential run whose load-bearing claims all describe galley itself from a code-generated specification and bypassed external verification—with no external seeds, baselines, single-family ablations, specificity controls, or final-prose audits—surprising_and_certain remains at 0, while seed-level system sprawl keeps cheap_to_adopt and conventional_body_one_graft at 1. Under the multiplicative standard, the manuscript should be reformulated around a focused, standalone scope-elastic verification/revision study backed by external-seed benchmarks and baselines before going out.

brief.concern: The author seems to want a valuable but rough idea to reach a high-impact, submission-ready paper without the labor, friction and gatekeeping of manual academic writing getting in the way.
brief.contribution: Galley is an editor in which agents from several model families take a text seed and produce a pre-publication academic manuscript through a chain of atomic behaviors, each proven in turn, with agent review-and-fix loops, tasks that can be assigned to humans or agents, citation choice and human provenance.
brief.field: Computer science: AI-assisted scientific writing and multi-agent LLM systems (human-computer interaction / metascience)
brief.audience: Researchers and engineers who build LLM-based multi-agent research and writing tools, metascience researchers who study what makes papers high-impact, and academic authors who want AI-assisted manuscript production

factors.name: input_not_output
factors.evidence: The project delivers a working capability in @autonomio/galley 0.1.0 under an MIT licence (https://github.com/autonomio/galley), along with structured provenance artifacts (a claim ledger, production record, sign-off sheet, and Resolvent evidence package). However, as stated in the seed (C3, C7, C10, C20, C26), the contribution is framed largely as an engineering account of one tightly coupled application stack (galley, poise, canary, and resolvent) and a single self-produced manuscript, rather than a tool-agnostic coordinate system, benchmark, or verification standard that researchers can apply directly with tools they already own. Moreover, transforming text alone (C5, C9) cannot supply missing empirical data or domain instruments.
factors.improve: Extract and formalize the epistemic accountability protocol—the claim ledger schema, code-enforced verbatim source grounding, planted-defect verifier calibration (calibrate), and non-self-review adjudication—as a standalone standard or evaluation benchmark alongside the open-source package so other systems can adopt it independently of Galley's full pipeline.

factors.name: shared_bottleneck
factors.evidence: The supplied material identifies two real bottlenecks, though key magnitudes remain unknown. For authors, 145,480 works match manuscript burden and 9,126 match gatekeeping, with studies documenting barriers for 320 surveyed scholars across 12 sub-Saharan African universities (W7223700638), 46 interviewed qualitative transportation participants (W4409382408), non-native English-speaking researchers (W4387029265), and racially and culturally minoritized scholars in Australia (W4413431338); however, the total number of blocked authors and the effect of writing automation on publication barriers and impact are unknown in the supplied results. For AI writing builders and users, the field's consensus explicitly flags claim–citation alignment and evaluating generated-paper quality as unresolved bottlenecks. Yet the seed's framing—turning a rough "rant" into "thousands of papers with high-impact potential" without manual labor (C9, C22)—targets raw prose drafting (already automated by 2026 tools) rather than the epistemic trust and empirical substance bottlenecks that actually block high-impact publication.
factors.improve: Drop the framing of mass-producing high-impact papers from raw rants (C9, C22) and anchor the paper squarely on the shared bottleneck confirmed in the literature: making AI-assisted scholarly manuscripts source-grounded, resistant to single-model self-review bias, and transparently auditable by authors and reviewers.

factors.name: conventional_body_one_graft
factors.evidence: While the topic fits the host field's questions and 2026 literature (PaperOrchestra, PaperDebugger, ResearchOS, DeepSciVerify, and multi-model review benchmarks) and imports a promising software-engineering pattern from autonomio/poise (replayable atomic behaviors divided into a required skeleton and non-blocking improvers), the seed violates the single-graft principle. It simultaneously bundles poise editor mechanics (C2, C3, C13, C19), canary systematic review (C7, C8), resolvent packaging (C10), a seven-factor metascience theory of impact (C1, C6), multi-family role separation (C18), planted-defect calibration, mixed-initiative @both commenting (C14–C17), and software-testing rules ("sunk-cost testing" in C23), wrapped in house-specific terminology.
factors.improve: Write the body entirely in standard CS, HCI, and metascience terminology—comparing directly against 2026 multi-agent writing and verification baselines—and organize the paper around one clean cross-domain graft, such as institutional separation of powers across independent model families enforced by a deterministic, fault-tolerant state machine.

factors.name: surprising_and_certain
factors.evidence: Neither half of "improbable beforehand, undeniable afterwards, holding up in strangers' hands" holds under the seed's claims and validation design. First, multi-agent conversion of pre-writing materials into manuscripts and in-editor revision is already established in 2026 prior art (PaperOrchestra, PaperDebugger) and current consensus, so end-to-end draft generation is not improbable beforehand. Second, the seed's surprising claims—that from a text input or "rant" alone the system yields a high-quality paper with projected high-impact potential (C5, C9, C22) and supports human-agent task and citation control (C14–C17)—have no certainty in strangers' hands: validation (C26, C27) relies on a single (N=1) autonomous self-referential run about Galley itself where accurate ground-truth system metadata is injected outside the seed, human-in-the-loop controls are unexercised (dial autonomous, citations auto), no external topics or strangers test the tool, no baselines are compared, citations are checked only against OpenAlex abstracts rather than full texts, calibrate metrics are unknown before execution, and evaluating generated-paper quality and research impact remains an open, unknown problem in the supplied literature.
factors.improve: Replace claims of universal high-impact generation from rants (C5, C9, C22) with a falsifiable epistemic-containment thesis—that cross-family non-self-review, verbatim passage verification, planted-defect calibration, and automatic claim narrowing/hedging bound unsupported overclaiming—and evaluate it across diverse external seeds, single-family and 2026 prior-art baselines, full-text checks, and human-in-the-loop user studies; if constrained to this autonomous run, explicitly scope the self-compilation as an instrumented glass-box case study and failure audit rather than proof of generalizable impact.

factors.name: opens_more_than_closes
factors.evidence: Because Galley is MIT-licensed, records deterministic replayable prompt-and-answer journals across model families, narrows or rejects claims against verbatim OpenAlex abstract passages, runs inline planted-defect calibration (calibrate), and emits machine-readable claim ledgers and Resolvent packages, it offers researchers concrete hooks to study cross-family vs. single-family review bias, abstract-vs.-full-text drift, and mixed-initiative authorship. However, pitching the work as a turnkey system that produces finished papers with no manual intervention (C9, C20, C22, C27) presents a closed automation product rather than foregrounding open empirical questions.
factors.improve: Frame the replayable production journal, claim ledger, and calibration loop as open research instruments, and structure the analysis around concrete failure modes—where abstract-only verification forces claim narrowing, where cross-family referees deadlock into third-family adjudication, and where pre-writing impact scoring diverges from evidentiary support—so readers immediately see follow-up experiments.

factors.name: cheap_to_adopt
factors.evidence: Although @autonomio/galley 0.1.0 is open-source under an MIT licence, the seed fails the three criteria of cheap adoption: "Galley" names an application rather than a conceptual noun the field lacks; it presents a 24-behavior feature inventory spanning poise, canary, and resolvent rather than one portable idea; and adopting the system outside its original setting requires configuring multiple frontier model family CLI clients (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon), Canary/OpenAlex search, and Typst across a long, multi-round pipeline.
factors.improve: Introduce one crisp conceptual noun for the core mechanism (for example, cross-family epistemic compilation or calibrated claim ledgers), distill that single principle out of the 24-step engineering bundle, and show how any research workflow can adopt the verification-and-ledger pattern without deploying the entire multi-provider editor stack.

factors.name: early
factors.evidence: While multi-agent research automation sits on a recent growth curve (17 matched works in 2025 and 23 in 2026) enabled by capable frontier models, the seed's headline pitch is already partly anticipated by five 2026 works: PaperOrchestra (end-to-end automated paper writing), PaperDebugger (in-editor multi-agent review and editing), ResearchOS (findings-to-claims compilation), DeepSciVerify (claim–citation verification), and a multi-model benchmark of AI scientists. Pitching an autonomous text-to-manuscript generator and editor places the paper behind that initial 2026 wave rather than at its base; only the narrower angle of cross-family constitutional governance and audit-grade provenance sits early on an emerging curve.
factors.improve: Concede upfront that multi-agent manuscript drafting and in-editor review are established in 2026, and reposition the contribution at the base of the next curve: enforceable epistemic governance, cross-family separation of powers, and verifiable human sign-off provenance for AI-assisted scholarship.

ideaReview.ceiling: If this works perfectly, builders of multi-agent scientific writing and discovery tools (the community behind systems such as PaperOrchestra, PaperDebugger, ResearchOS, and DeepSciVerify) stop allowing a model family to verify or referee its own drafted claims and adopt cross-family separation of powers, code-confirmed verbatim passage grounding, inline planted-defect verifier calibration, and machine-readable claim ledgers as standard architectural gates. Academic authors—including scholars facing documented manuscript burden and linguistic or institutional publication barriers—use mixed-initiative task sharing, per-claim citation choice, and explicit sign-off sheets to turn rough research notes into transparently audited manuscripts whose unsupported claims are narrowed or marked as hypotheses rather than silently fabricated. Preprint moderators, journal editors, and metascience researchers shift from post-hoc prose policing to inspecting shipped claim ledgers, cross-family adjudication records, and production journals during peer review.
ideaReview.summary: As stated in the seed, the idea fails on surprising_and_certain (0) and scores weakly on conventional_body_one_graft (1), cheap_to_adopt (1), and early (1). In 2026, end-to-end multi-agent manuscript generation and in-editor review are already established by PaperOrchestra and PaperDebugger, so demonstrating that agents can assemble a formatted draft is no longer surprising beforehand. Meanwhile, the seed's bold claims—that given only a text seed or "rant," the system yields high-impact scientific papers at the scale of thousands of papers (C5, C9, C22) while supporting flexible human-agent collaboration (C14–C17)—have no certainty in strangers' hands: the validation plan (C26, C27) rests on a single autonomous, self-referential run about Galley itself with code-injected accurate system metadata, disabled human-in-the-loop steps, abstract-only citation checks, unknown pre-run calibration numbers, and no external seeds or baseline comparisons. However, a strong paper can come from reformulating the same underlying concern: drop the indefensible promise of mass-producing high-impact science from rants, strip internal ecosystem jargon into one clean cross-domain graft, and center the manuscript on Galley's genuinely distinctive architecture—cross-family separation of powers (no model family reviews its own work), code-confirmed verbatim source grounding with explicit claim narrowing and hedging, inline planted-defect verifier calibration, and auditable claim ledgers and human sign-off sheets—treating the autonomous self-compilation honestly as an instrumented glass-box audit rather than universal proof of research impact.

selectedDirection.reason: D1 keeps the full Galley editor and its high-impact aim while giving the paper one reusable contribution: keep drafting when evidence falls short, narrow or hedge the affected claims, and record their disposition for audit. Galley’s autonomous self-run can show whether that mechanism works end to end in this case. Its performance on outside seeds and its effect on long-run impact remain unknown.

plan.thesis: Treating claim scope, rather than manuscript completion, as the thing verification acts on lets a multi-family compiler carry a rough text seed to a complete pre-publication manuscript without blocking gates. Any claim that goes beyond its verified evidence is narrowed, stated as a hypothesis, or sent to the authors for sign-off, and is not stated as established fact.
plan.workingTitle: Scope-Elastic Manuscript Compilation: Narrowing Claims Instead of Blocking Drafts or Fabricating Support
opens: A scope-fidelity benchmark: seeds with planted overclaims, scored on whether a compiler narrows, hedges or passes each one, run against single-family pipelines and prior end-to-end writing systems.
Abstract-versus-full-text drift: how often claims verified against OpenAlex abstracts are contradicted or narrowed further when checked against full texts.
Cross-family versus same-family verification: using planted-defect calibration and replayable journals to measure self-preference in citation verification and referee adjudication.
Mixed-initiative sign-off studies: whether authors and reviewers working from a claim ledger and sign-off sheet catch more overclaims, with less effort, than people reading the prose alone.
The claim ledger as an interchange format: auditing the claim scope of human-written papers and preprints with the same ledger schema.
Across many external seeds, testing whether reformulating a seed against impact heuristics before writing changes how reviewers and readers rate the resulting manuscripts.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Sets out the problem. Authors with a valuable but rough idea face the labour and gatekeeping of manual writing, and AI writing tools either halt on pass/fail verification gates or smooth unsupported assertions into fluent prose. States the thesis, introduces galley as an editor-integrated multi-family manuscript compiler, and lists the contributions with pointers to the sections that establish them.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.purpose: Places galley among multi-agent writing systems, claim–citation verifiers, evaluations of AI-generated papers, findings on self-preference in LLM evaluators, and metascience on features of high-impact papers. Ends by stating which combination is new and which parts earlier work established.

sections.title: Scope-Elastic Compilation
sections.purpose: Defines scope-elastic compilation. Completion is held fixed by a small set of required behaviours, claim scope is what verification acts on, and a claim that goes beyond its evidence has exactly three permitted outcomes. Grounds narrowing and hedging in the academic-writing account of hedging and extends elasticity from single claims to the thesis.

sections.title: Galley: Ladder, Scheduler and Seats
sections.purpose: Describes the ladder of 24 atomic behaviours (7 required, 17 improvers), the scheduler that rescans from the top, how failures and outages are handled without stopping the paper, and how seats are assigned across model families so that no family reviews its own work. Covers the pre-writing challenge of the seed and the post-review rescoring, both described as heuristic self-assessments.

sections.title: Evidence, Verification and Claim Scope
sections.purpose: Follows a claim from evidence search to final standing: retrieval through Canary over OpenAlex, the code check that passages are verbatim and records come from the DOI registry, the cross-family verdicts that support, narrow or reject a citation, drafting that cites only verified passages, the fidelity rewrite, per-run calibration of the verifier, and the reconcile pass that brings the ledger into line with the final text.

sections.title: Review, Human Participation and the Manuscript Package
sections.purpose: Describes the rotating cross-family referee seats, the capped answer-and-judge loop with third-family adjudication, and stored prompts and answers that allow replay. Sets out the optional human controls (direct edits, routed comment threads, proposed edits, a/b/c citation choice, the dial) and the full output package with its claim ledger, Resolvent evidence package, production record and sign-off sheet.

sections.title: Case Study: The Run That Produced This Manuscript
sections.purpose: Reports the instrumented case study of the single autonomous run that compiled this manuscript from the authors' seed with two referee rounds for a preprint venue. From the production record and claim ledger it gives counts of claims supported, narrowed, stated as hypotheses or dropped, the improvers skipped, the planted defects the verifier caught, and how referee findings were resolved. All values come from the generated production record, and the models add no numbers.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.purpose: States the limits of the evidence. There is one self-referential run, with no external seeds and no single-family or prior-system baselines. The human-in-the-loop controls were not used, verification read only abstracts, and the impact scores are heuristic self-assessments. 'Ready for submission' means every gate held on one revision, not that the claims are correct or that the paper will have impact.

sections.title: What This Opens
sections.purpose: Names the research that scope-elastic compilation makes possible. Directions include a scope-fidelity benchmark with planted overclaims, abstract-versus-full-text drift, cross-family versus same-family verification measured through calibration and replay, mixed-initiative sign-off studies, the claim ledger as an interchange format for auditing human-written papers, and tests of pre-writing reformulation across external seeds. Closes with the open-source release.

outline.style: Venue and form: an arXiv preprint in cs.DL, written as a systems paper with an instrumented case study, in the register of HCI and metascience writing on LLM tools. Voice: first-person plural 'we' for the authors, active voice, short declarative sentences, one idea per paragraph with the point in the first sentence. Use present tense for what galley does and past tense for what happened in this run. Names: write 'galley' in lowercase as the package name and capitalise it only at the start of a sentence. Write poise, Canary, OpenAlex and Resolvent as given. Give the release once as @autonomio/galley 0.1.0 (MIT licence) with its repository URL. At first mention give each model's name with its model ID in parentheses, and use the short name after that. Set behaviour names in monospace (`extract`, `verify`, `fidelity`, `reconcile`, ...) exactly as they appear on the ladder. Seat names (author, checker, challenger, verifier, referee, adjudicator) are plain text. Spelling is British throughout (behaviour, licence, favourably), matching the claims. Terms: define 'scope-elastic compilation' once in S3 and use no variants. The only words for claim outcomes are supported, narrowed, stated as a hypothesis, dropped, and listed for sign-off; never use synonyms such as softened or weakened. In prose, say 'required behaviour' and mention 'skeleton' once as its synonym. Evidence: cite only verified passages, with numeric bracketed citations. Background claims that end without verified evidence are written as explicit hypotheses. Galley's mechanics are stated as the authors' own work, without citation. Never invent references for poise or Canary. Do not list or name the seven impact factors, because the source material does not enumerate them, and always call the scores heuristic self-assessments, not predictions. Numbers: every value from the run comes from the generated production record (run.* placeholders) and appears in one table in S7. Prose refers to that table and never restates values approximately. Durations carry units (hours) and counts are exact. Do not report the effect of writing automation on barriers to publication, because it is unknown, and say so where it is raised. Self-reference: state plainly that this manuscript is galley's first production and the subject of the case study. Make no claims of generality, superiority over baselines or future impact. Lists: only the contributions in S1 and the open directions in S9 may be numbered lists; everything else is prose. Refer to figures as Figure 1–3. Excluded vocabulary: none of the banned hype or filler words, no rhetorical questions, no addressing the reader.
glossary: scope-elastic compilation: manuscript compilation that holds completion fixed through a small set of required behaviours and makes each claim's scope the object of verification, so that a claim exceeding its verified evidence is narrowed, stated as a hypothesis or listed for human sign-off, and is never blocked or stated as established fact
galley: the authors' editor-integrated manuscript compiler in which agents from several model families carry a text seed to a pre-publication manuscript package
seed: the written text a person supplies as the sole required input to a galley run; spoken input is out of scope
claim: a single assertion in the claim graph set by plan, marked as needing external evidence, as the authors' own work, or as a premise
load-bearing claim: a claim the thesis depends on; if it ends without evidence, reassess decides whether the thesis stands, narrows or fails
claim scope: the extent of what a claim asserts, which verification may reduce to match its evidence
narrowing: reducing a claim's scope to what a verified passage states
hypothesis (stated as a hypothesis): the explicit hedged form given to a claim that has no verified evidence
ladder: the ordered list of 24 atomic behaviours that the scheduler scans from the top
atomic behaviour: a unit of work that reads the paper's state, does one thing and writes its result, without knowing what comes next
required behaviour (skeleton): one of the seven behaviours (extract, plan, outline, draft, frame, typeset, ready) that make a paper exist
improver: one of the 17 behaviours that can make the paper better but never stop it; after two failures it is skipped and its effect recorded
scheduler: the component that runs whatever behaviour is ready and rescans the ladder from the top whenever anything settles
model family: a group of models from one provider, each run through its own command-line client with no tools and no delegation, answering in a strict JSON schema
seat: a role assigned to a model family (author, checker, challenger, verifier, referee, adjudicator), arranged so that no family reviews its own work
candidate passage: a text span that code confirms is copied verbatim from a cited work's abstract and that is proposed as evidence for a claim
Canary: the authors' literature search tool over OpenAlex, which keeps retrieval outside galley
verdict: the verifier's judgement of a candidate passage against its claim as supported, narrower or not supported
fidelity: the behaviour that checks each drafted section against its claims and rewrites sentences that say more than their evidence
calibration: the behaviour that plants defective citations and unaltered controls among verified ones and measures how many the verifier catches
reconcile: the post-review pass in which a family other than the author's confirms, narrows or drops each ledger claim against the final text
claim ledger: the table ending each manuscript that lists every claim with its kind, standing, origin in the seed or the system, and sources
standing: a claim's final status in the ledger (supported, narrowed, stated as a hypothesis, or dropped)
evidence package: the per-paper archive of claims, evidence and sources in the Resolvent format
sign-off sheet: the list of what only the authors can decide: declarations, claims the system added, claims stated as hypotheses, decisions a third family made, and skipped steps
production record: the account of the run generated from its journal and included in the manuscript
production journal: the stored record of every prompt and answer, which allows a rerun to replay the process without calling a model
finding: a referee's report on the manuscript, carrying a severity and the decision it asks for
adjudication: settlement of a finding still disputed after the answer cap, by the family that is neither author nor referee
dial: the setting that controls whether load-bearing citations and critical answers, every answer, or no step waits for a person; autonomous in this run
@humans / @both: comment-thread routing in which the person keeps the thread, or shares it with the agents and receives proposed edits to accept or decline
citation choice: an optional mode in which each claim waits for the person to choose among candidate sources (a, b, c), let the system pick, or state the claim without a source
impact-factor scores: heuristic self-assessments of an idea or finished paper on seven impact factors, made by review-idea and reprofile; they are not predictions of impact

ready: the final required behaviour, which marks the paper ready for submission once every gate holds on one revision; it does not certify that the claims are correct or that the paper will have impact
poise: the authors' earlier tool for semi-autonomous software engineering, the source of the atomic-behaviour pattern and the in-editor side-chat pattern

frame.title: Scope-Elastic Manuscript Compilation Narrows or Hedges Unsupported Claims Instead of Blocking Drafts
frame.abstract: Systems that automate academic writing must handle claims that exceed their evidence. A pass/fail verification gate can halt the draft, and unchecked generation can present unsupported assertions as fact. We define scope-elastic compilation: required behaviours complete the manuscript, and a claim exceeding its verified evidence is narrowed, given hypothesis standing or listed for author sign-off; the draft continues. We present galley, an open-source compiler in which agents from several model families carry a text seed to a pre-publication manuscript through 24 atomic behaviours: 7 required and 17 improvers that cannot stop the paper. Code confirms that each cited passage appears verbatim in its source's abstract and lets the draft cite only verified passages. One family proposes each passage; another judges it against its claim. Whether prose respects claim standing rests on drafting instructions and post-draft model checks that can miss overclaims or be skipped. Each run writes a claim ledger, an evidence package and a sign-off sheet. A case study of the autonomous run that compiled this manuscript reports review-stage counts: {{run.claims}} ledger claims, {{run.claims_narrowed}} narrowed and {{run.claims_unsupported}} given hypothesis standing, provisional until reconciliation, and {{run.calibration}} planted defects caught, a measure of sensitivity only. Most claims describe galley itself and bypass literature verification; one self-referential run with abstract-only verification and no external seeds or baselines cannot show that galley generalises. The work opens a scope-fidelity benchmark with planted overclaims, cross-family versus same-family verification studies, and ledger-based audits of human-written papers.

factors.name: input_not_output
factors.evidence: The paper releases an open-source capability (@autonomio/galley 0.1.0 under MIT), defines the conceptual frame of scope-elastic compilation (Section 3), and introduces structured provenance outputs—the claim ledger, Resolvent evidence package, sign-off sheet, and deterministic replay journal (Sections 2, 6). However, it delivers no validated coordinate system: the scope-fidelity benchmark is only proposed as future work (Section 9), the seven-factor heuristic scores are unvalidated (Sections 2, 4), calibrate omits control counts and defect-construction rules (Section 5), and Section 7 reports findings on one self-referential run of one system rather than demonstrating a tool verified to work across external users' inputs.
factors.improve: Build and release the Section 9.1 scope-fidelity benchmark—complete with external seeds containing planted overclaims of known narrower scope, supported controls, and automated scoring—alongside standalone schemas and validators for claim ledgers and sign-off sheets tested across multiple writing systems.

factors.name: shared_bottleneck
factors.evidence: Verified citations establish that claim–citation misalignment is a recurring failure mode in LLM-generated scientific reports (@sadeghi2026deepsciverif) and that AI-generated papers still contain more unsupported claims and affirmative front-section citations even when retrieval and human guidance reduce ghost citations (@oh2026show), while automated paper review (@ravideshik2026can) and evaluator self-preference (@chen2025beyond; @daneshjou2026judge) remain active concerns. However, Section 1 explicitly states that it does not assess how often existing tools actually halt drafts at pass/fail gates versus emitting unchecked prose, and galley's abstract-only verification (Section 8) leaves researchers' deeper bottleneck—verifying claims against full texts, methods, and empirical results—unaddressed.
factors.improve: Quantify the bottleneck directly by auditing outputs from existing automated manuscript generators and retrieval-augmented writing tools to measure how often failed verification blocks completion versus letting unsupported claims pass as established fact.

factors.name: conventional_body_one_graft
factors.evidence: The manuscript situates itself in AI-generated scientific writing and citation verification (@song2026paperorchest; @lu2024scientist; @sadeghi2026deepsciverif; @oh2026show) and grafts semi-autonomous software-engineering scheduling from poise (skeleton versus non-blocking improvers) together with academic hedging (@alshbeekat2025hedging) to treat verification as scope adjustment rather than a boolean gate. Yet the host-field body is thin—resting on only 10 cited works total—and Section 2 explicitly omits retrieval-grounded long-form writing, post-hoc factual revision of LLM outputs outside scientific writing, interactive human–AI writing editors, and digital-library provenance models, while mixing multiple disparate mechanisms (compiler metaphors, hedging pragmatics, cross-family LLM judging, and citation-atypicality metascience @uzzi2013atypical; @mukherjee2017atypical) rather than executing one deep graft into a thorough literature base.
factors.improve: Ground the conventional body thoroughly in NLP literature on retrieval-grounded generation, post-hoc claim revision/editing, selective abstention, and scholarly provenance, and strip away secondary threads (such as unvalidated metascience idea scoring) to sharpen a single formal graft from fault-tolerant compilation onto claim-standing revision.

factors.name: surprising_and_certain
factors.evidence: The manuscript is neither surprising beforehand nor empirically certain afterwards. Conceptually, hedging or flagging unverified claims for human review is an intuitive engineering fallback, and even the four-part system novelty is stated only as an abstract-based hypothesis (Section 2; C42). Empirically, certainty in strangers' hands is untested: the sole evaluation is a single, self-referential, review-stage snapshot of galley compiling this manuscript (Sections 7, 8) using a code-generated specification unavailable to outside users. In Appendix A, 26 of 38 ledger claims—and all 14 load-bearing claims—describe the authors' own work and bypassed external search and verification; reassess never ran; calibrate (6 of 6 planted defects caught) omits unaltered control counts and verdicts, leaving specificity/false-rejection rates unknown (Section 5); no single-family ablation, prior-system baseline, external seed, or human-in-the-loop run was tested (Section 8); and code enforces only verbatim abstract provenance, not prose scope (Section 3). Even within this snapshot, Appendix A holds both an unverified hypothesis (C28) and a narrowed claim (C43) for PaperOrchestra while Section 2 states the broader 'unconstrained... LaTeX' wording as fact (without the source abstract in the request, whether prose exceeded evidence or C28 is an unreconciled duplicate is unknown, illustrating that final-text scope fidelity remains unverified).
factors.improve: Run controlled evaluations on diverse external seeds from independent authors (without code-generated system specifications) comparing galley against unchecked generation, hard pass/fail verification gates, single-family ablations, and prior systems (@song2026paperorchest; @sadeghi2026deepsciverif), reporting control-calibrated sensitivity and specificity plus blinded human audits of final-prose fidelity against full texts.

factors.name: opens_more_than_closes
factors.evidence: Section 9 specifies six concrete follow-up studies, notably a scope-fidelity benchmark with planted overclaims and supported controls (measuring both unhedged overclaiming and unnecessary hedging), a crossed multi-family versus same-family verifier replay design that holds candidate passages and controls fixed, abstract-versus-full-text drift measurement, and ledger-based auditing of human-written manuscripts. Storing prompts, answers, and replayable journals in an open-source package makes follow-up inspection practical. However, most of these six studies represent the missing primary validation of galley's own design assumptions rather than new territory unlocked by an established empirical finding.
factors.improve: Complete the core scope-fidelity benchmark and crossed family-separation study within this paper, and publish a multi-domain dataset of replayable production journals, verified abstract/full-text pairs, and reconciled claim ledgers so others can build new methods on top of a proven baseline.

factors.name: cheap_to_adopt
factors.evidence: The manuscript coins a clear phrase—scope-elastic compilation—alongside reusable artifact concepts (claim ledger, sign-off sheet) and MIT-licensed code. However, it fails the 'one idea' test: Section 2 and C42 explicitly define novelty as a four-element conjunction, while Sections 4 and 6 retain extensive seed baggage (24 atomic behaviours, @humans/@both editor comment threads from poise, 6-hour and 3-hour outage timers, spoken-input exclusions, and seven-factor heuristic rescoring). Technical adoption outside galley's original setting is also heavy, requiring separate command-line clients across three frontier model families (120 calls and 2.6M input / 1.735M output tokens for one run), Canary over OpenAlex, and academic abstract/DOI structure, while the term 'compilation' risks overstating enforcement when narrowing and prose fidelity rely on skippable model judgments.
factors.improve: Factor out the scope-elastic claim verifier, narrower, and claim-ledger/sign-off generator as a lightweight, model-agnostic standalone library usable in any grounded text-generation pipeline without the 24-behaviour editor, multi-CLI setup, or Canary dependency, and trim orthogonal editor mechanics from the paper.

factors.name: early
factors.evidence: Automated scientific paper generation and claim–citation verification form an active, still-developing area with open evaluation challenges (cited works span 2024–2026). Nonetheless, multi-agent end-to-end manuscript generation and simulated review already predate galley (@lu2024scientist; @song2026paperorchest), dedicated two-stage scientific claim–citation verification that escalates from abstracts to full-text passages already exists (@sadeghi2026deepsciverif), and LLM evaluator self-preference is already documented (@chen2025beyond; @daneshjou2026judge). Because galley checks abstracts only rather than full texts and combines existing capabilities into an incremental workflow rather than exploiting a newly unlocked instrument, it sits mid-wave rather than at the base of a new growth curve.
factors.improve: Target the genuinely nascent frontier where existing verifiers and writers still lack structure—such as passage-level and artifact-level (code, tables, experimental logs) scope-elastic compilation that reconciles prose claims directly against executable outputs and full-text evidence.

profileAfter.ceiling: Under the multiplicative standard, the 0 on surprising_and_certain (compounded by 1s on conventional_body_one_graft, cheap_to_adopt, and early) caps the manuscript's long-run impact at a transparent engineering report and open-source reference artifact for the niche community building automated paper-writing pipelines. Without external seeds, prior-system or single-family baselines, specificity controls, or an audit showing that final prose actually stays within verified evidence, outside researchers have no empirical proof that scope-elastic compilation works in strangers' hands, preventing broad adoption or field-level impact.
profileAfter.summary: Compared with the pre-draft profile (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1), the finished manuscript retains the exact same score vector (2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1). Reframing around scope-elastic compilation (Section 3; C34–C40) and maintaining scrupulous candour about enforcement boundaries and limitations (Sections 3, 5, 7, 8) produced an honest, coherent architectural account, an open-source package, and crisp follow-up designs (Section 9). However, honesty about missing evidence does not substitute for evidence: because the sole evaluation is a provisional, self-referential run whose load-bearing claims all describe galley itself from a code-generated specification and bypassed external verification—with no external seeds, baselines, single-family ablations, specificity controls, or final-prose audits—surprising_and_certain remains at 0, while seed-level system sprawl keeps cheap_to_adopt and conventional_body_one_graft at 1. Under the multiplicative standard, the manuscript should be reformulated around a focused, standalone scope-elastic verification/revision study backed by external-seed benchmarks and baselines before going out.

editorBase.S1:
This paper considers how authors can develop a promising but rough idea into a pre-publication manuscript. Authors face the labour of manuscript preparation and the gatekeeping of academic publishing. We aim to reduce that labour while keeping manuscript claims within the scope of the evidence.



A design choice in manuscript automation is how to handle claims that exceed their evidence. One design puts pass/fail verification gates in the path of the draft. A claim that fails verification can halt the draft. Another design generates fluent prose without checking individual claims. In this design, an unsupported assertion can read as established fact. Section 2 reviews prior work on claim–citation verification. We do not assess how often existing tools follow either pattern. 

 Our thesis is that a compiler can use verification to set the scope of claims while agents from several model families carry a rough text seed through to a pre-publication manuscript. At drafting, when a claim needs external evidence, the compiler narrows the claim to what a verified source passage states, writes it as a hypothesis if no passage supports it, or holds it back when a person chooses citations. The compiler does not check claims about the authors' own work or premises against the literature. The authors' sign-off sheet lists every hypothesis and every claim that the system, rather than the seed, added. After drafting, fidelity checking and review revise prose that exceeds its claims or evidence, and reconciliation aligns the claim ledger with the final text. Judgments of support and wording rest on models. If a post-drafting step fails twice, the compiler skips it and lists the skip on the sign-off sheet, so an overclaiming sentence can remain in the completed manuscript until the authors act on that sheet. We call this approach scope-elastic compilation, and Section 3 defines it.

Galley implements this design in an editor. Our case study examines the autonomous run that produced this manuscript, in which no step waited for a person. The run took two inputs: the authors' text seed, which sets what the paper argues, and a description of galley generated from its ladder, seats and package metadata, which supplies how galley works.        

      

This paper makes the following contributions:

1. We define scope-elastic compilation, in which required behaviours carry the manuscript to completion and verification sets the scope of each claim rather than gating completion (Section 3).
2. We describe galley's ladder of 24 atomic behaviours, 7 required and 17 that can improve the paper but never stop it, and the role-pair rules that assign different model families across specific seat pairs: direction proposer and selector, citation checker and verifier, author and referee, author and ledger reconciler, and an adjudicator distinct from both author and referee (Section 4).  
3. We describe how evidence revises claims: code confirms that each cited passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract, and a model family other than the proposer's judges whether the passage supports the claim, supports a narrower claim, or does not support it (Section 5). 
4. We describe cross-family referee review, optional human participation, and the claim ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet that each run produces (Section 6). 
5. We report a case study of manuscript production with galley (Section 7).
editorBase.S2:
We place galley among five strands of work: automated systems that write papers, verifiers of claim–citation alignment, evaluations of AI-generated papers, measurements of self-preference in LLM evaluators, and metascience on what distinguishes high-impact papers.

## Automated writing systems

Automated systems already carry research material to a finished paper. PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing that transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including literature synthesis and generated visuals [@song2026paperorchest]. The AI Scientist generates research ideas, writes code, runs experiments, writes a full scientific paper and evaluates it in a simulated review process [@lu2024scientist]. Multi-agent drafting and automated review therefore predate galley. The comparison set does not include retrieval-grounded long-form writing systems or interactive human–AI writing editors, and we do not propose galley's in-editor collaboration as new. We address a different question: what a compiler does with a claim that its evidence does not cover.

## Claim–citation verification

Misalignment between claims and their cited evidence is a common failure mode in reports generated by large language models [@sadeghi2026deepsciverif]. Even when retrieval and human guidance reduce ghost citations, AI-generated papers contain more unsupported claims, rely on front-section evidence and use citations more affirmatively [@oh2026show]. DeepSciVerify verifies scientific claim–citation alignment in two stages: it reasons over abstracts and escalates selectively to passage-level evidence [@sadeghi2026deepsciverif]. Galley does not propose claim–citation verification or retrieval-supported citation as a contribution. Galley's proposed contribution is the action it takes on a claim after each verdict. Galley verifies against less text than DeepSciVerify: code confirms that each passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract, and no step escalates to the full text. A verifier from a family other than the checker's judges each passage against its claim. A supported claim keeps its scope, a claim the passage covers in part is narrowed to what the passage states, and a rejected citation gives way to the next candidate. A claim that no abstract supports, including one that only a full text would support, is stated as a hypothesis while manuscript preparation continues.

## Evaluating AI-generated papers

Evaluating and comparing the quality of AI-generated research papers remains an open challenge; a benchmarking protocol assesses such papers with an LLM-based automated peer-review system on originality, scientific rigour, clarity and significance [@ravideshik2026can]. That protocol evaluates papers after a system has generated them. Galley uses referees from several model families during production, and the author revises the manuscript in answer to their findings. 

## Self-preference in LLM evaluators

LLMs used as evaluators tend to rate their own outputs more favourably than outputs from other models [@chen2025beyond; @daneshjou2026judge]. The cited passages report a model's preference for its own outputs, not a preference among models of one family; separating families on a role pair excludes both. Galley addresses this risk on specific role pairs rather than across all contributions: it assigns different model families to direction proposer and selector, citation checker and verifier, author and referee, author and ledger reconciler, and an adjudicator distinct from both author and referee (Section 4). Outside those pairs, a family can evaluate material to which it contributed in an earlier role. Whether these role-pair rules reduce self-preference in galley remains an open question.

## Features of high-impact papers

An analysis of 17.9 million papers across all scientific fields suggested that the highest-impact papers are primarily grounded in exceptionally conventional combinations of prior work while also featuring an intrusion of unusual combinations [@uzzi2013atypical; @mukherjee2017atypical]. Findings of this kind motivate assessing an idea before writing it, but atypicality in this sense is a property of a finished reference list, which a seed does not yet have. Galley's review-idea behavior scores the idea on seven impact factors before drafting, and its reprofile behavior scores the finished paper. Neither behavior measures reference-combination atypicality, and the seven factors have not been validated as predictors of impact.

## Provenance records

Each run writes three provenance records alongside the manuscript. The claim ledger lists every claim with its kind, its standing, whether the seed or the system made it, and its sources. The evidence package holds the claims, the verbatim abstract passages that support them and their sources in the Resolvent format, and a cited work with a DOI takes its bibliographic record from the DOI registry. The production journal, with every stored prompt and answer, lets a rerun replay each step without calling a model. We present these records as outputs of galley's workflow and do not compare them with digital-library models of citation context or scholarly provenance.

## What is new

We state the novelty of galley as a hypothesis, because the abstract passages cited here summarize what each system does; they cannot show that no system, or no full paper of a cited system, combines the elements below. The comparison set is the closest prior systems whose abstracts we cite: PaperOrchestra and The AI Scientist for end-to-end writing, and DeepSciVerify for claim–citation verification. As far as we know, none of them combines four elements. The first is manuscript preparation that continues when an improver behavior fails and is skipped. The second is automatic narrowing or hedging of claims based on evidence that code checks against the cited source word for word. The third is cross-family verification, and the fourth is a human sign-off sheet. The novelty we propose lies in this combination, not in any one element. When a citation fails verification, the cited abstract passages of PaperOrchestra and The AI Scientist state no rule for the claim, and the passage cited for DeepSciVerify describes a verification pipeline, not a writer that revises the claim. In galley, the next candidate citation replaces a rejected one, and a claim left without verified evidence is stated as a hypothesis. The cited works establish multi-agent drafting, simulated review, automated paper evaluation and claim–citation verification, and post-hoc revision of language-model output outside scientific writing may anticipate the second element. Galley uses cross-family verification to adjust claim scope while manuscript preparation continues.
editorBase.S3:
We define scope-elastic compilation as follows. A manuscript compiler reaches completion through a small set of required behaviours and makes each claim's scope, rather than completion, the object that verification acts on. When a claim exceeds its verified evidence, the compiler narrows it to what the evidence supports, gives it hypothesis standing, or lists it for human sign-off instead of halting the draft. Three levels of this definition must be kept apart. Claim standing records what each claim may assert; the compiler sets it from verification outcomes, and the sign-off sheet lists each claim stated as a hypothesis. Drafting instructions direct the `draft` model to write each claim at its standing. Code enforcement covers only citations: `draft` can cite only passages that passed verification. Whether each sentence stays within its claim's standing is a model judgment, which post-draft checks review but cannot guarantee. Galley is our manuscript compiler.

The required behaviours form the skeleton and determine completion through three states. A draft exists once `draft` has written every section. A package exists once `frame` has written the title and abstract and `typeset` has rendered the manuscript, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet. The paper is complete once `ready` marks it ready for submission, which it does when every gate holds on one revision, so the text and all its outputs come from that revision. Every other behaviour is an improver: it can improve the paper but never stop it, and one that fails twice is skipped with its effect recorded. Because `verify` is an improver, no gate depends on a verification result, so verification verdicts never block completion while claim scope varies; a model provider's usage limit longer than about six hours, for example, still pauses the run, which can then be resumed.

Claim scope is the extent of what a claim asserts. A claim is supported when its verified evidence covers its scope; a claim whose scope exceeds that evidence has three permitted outcomes. Narrowing reduces the claim's scope to what the verified evidence supports: the narrowed claim asserts nothing the original did not. A revised claim that asserts something new is a substitution, even when the passage supports it, and the definition does not permit it. For a hypothetical example, a claim that a method improves recall on every benchmark, matched to a passage reporting an improvement on one benchmark, narrows to an improvement on that benchmark; replacing it with the passage's statement about runtime would be substitution. Stating the claim as a hypothesis marks it as tentative. Listing the claim for sign-off leaves the final decision to human judgment. Until a person decides, the claim keeps narrowed or hypothesis standing, or, with citation choices on, is held back from the draft. At claim assignment, the definition excludes two other outcomes: halting the draft over failed verification, and assigning supported standing to a claim whose evidence does not cover it.

We interpret the first two outcomes in terms of academic hedging. In academic writing, hedging is a way writers moderate the strength of a claim and their commitment to it [@alshbeekat2025hedging]. In support of previous literature, that study concludes that hedging devices qualify writers' commitment, lessen the impact of their claims and convey probability. We treat narrowing as a reduction in claim strength because it limits what the claim asserts. Stating the claim as a hypothesis preserves its content and expresses a weaker commitment to its truth. 

Verification selects the outcome. When the verifier judges a passage narrower than its claim, the compiler narrows the claim to what the passage states. Whether the narrowed claim asserts nothing beyond the original rests on model judgment; code does not check it. When a claim ends without a supported passage, it takes hypothesis standing, `draft` is instructed to state it as a hypothesis, and the sign-off sheet lists it. In the autonomous setting, the authors sign off after the manuscript is complete. If a person turns citation choices on, each claim is instead held back from the draft until they pick a candidate source, let the system pick, or state it without a source; the dial can make load-bearing citations wait in the same way. 

Elasticity also extends beyond single claims. Some claims are load-bearing: the thesis depends on them. When a load-bearing claim ends without evidence, the `reassess` behaviour decides whether the thesis stands, narrows or fails. Because `reassess` is an improver, even a fail verdict does not stop the paper: the load-bearing claim takes hypothesis standing like any other claim without a supported passage, and the sign-off sheet lists it.

Post-draft improvers review the prose and its records but do not enforce scope. The `fidelity` behaviour rewrites drafted sentences that say more than their evidence. During review, the referee who raised a finding judges each author answer and its edits, while `adjudicate` settles findings at the answer cap and lists its decisions on the sign-off sheet. After review, `reconcile` runs in a family other than the author's to align the claim ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet with the final text; it changes those records, not the prose. No required behaviour rechecks sentences or ledger entries after drafting. Code confirms that each cited passage appears verbatim in its source's abstract; passage support, sentence fidelity and ledger alignment are model judgments, and of these only the verifier's detection of planted defective citations is measured, by `calibrate`. A sentence that says more than its evidence, or a ledger entry that differs from the text, can therefore reach the completed manuscript in two ways. A post-draft improver that fails twice is skipped, and the sign-off sheet names the skipped step. A check that runs can miss the error, and nothing flags the miss. In both cases the error is left to the authors' review rather than to compiler enforcement.
editorBase.S4:
Galley turns one input into a manuscript. The input is a seed: a written text in which a person states an idea. Galley takes written text only, and spoken input is out of scope. With the dial set to autonomous, the person supplies only the seed and no step waits for a person. This section describes the ladder of behaviours, the scheduler, failure and outage handling, and seat assignments across model families. Section 5 follows a claim through the evidence behaviours, and Section 6 covers review.

## The ladder of behaviours

Galley breaks manuscript production into a ladder of 24 atomic behaviours. Seven are required behaviours, also called the skeleton: `extract`, `plan`, `outline`, `draft`, `frame`, `typeset` and `ready`. Together they make a paper exist. The other 17 behaviours are improvers. An improver can make the paper better but can never stop it.

The ladder orders the behaviours as follows. `extract` lists the seed's claims, the concern behind them, its stated contribution and its host field. Four improvers then aim the idea: `position` places it against its closest prior work, `review-idea` scores it, `reformulate` proposes new directions and `select-direction` chooses among them. `plan` sets the thesis and the claim graph, and `outline` sets the sections, word budgets and planned figures. Four improvers handle evidence: `find-evidence`, `verify`, `reassess` and `calibrate`. `draft` writes each section once its evidence is settled. The improvers `figure` and `fidelity` then draw the planned figures and check each drafted section against its claims. `frame` writes the title, abstract and keywords. Five improvers run review: `referee`, `close-round`, `respond`, `verify-disposition` and `adjudicate`. The improvers `reconcile` and `reprofile` then align the claim ledger with the final text and rescore the finished paper. `typeset` renders the outputs, and `ready` marks the paper ready for submission.

## Atomic behaviours and the scheduler

Galley takes the atomic-behaviour pattern from poise, our earlier tool for semi-autonomous software engineering. Each behaviour reads the paper's state, does one thing and writes its result. No behaviour knows what comes next. The scheduler determines the order of execution. The scheduler starts at the top of the ladder and returns to the top whenever work settles. The ladder order is therefore the order in which the scheduler considers behaviours, not a fixed sequence of steps.

After a later behaviour settles, the scheduler considers earlier behaviours again and runs any that are ready. Caps limit how often work repeats. In this run, review was capped at two referee rounds and at three answers per finding before a third family adjudicated it. A skipped improver still settles its part of the paper's state through its recorded effect, so the behaviours that wait on it can run. For example, `draft` writes a section once the evidence for its claims is settled. If `verify` fails twice, galley skips it, gives the affected claims hypothesis standing, lists the skip on the sign-off sheet, and instructs `draft` to state them as hypotheses.

Readiness ties the manuscript and its outputs to one revision, though the generated description of galley omits the individual gates and their predicates. `typeset` renders the outputs again whenever the text changes. `ready` marks the paper ready for submission only when every gate holds on one revision. Any later change to the text, from a referee answer or from a person's edit in the editor, makes a new revision on which every gate must hold again. Because improvers never stop the paper, no gate depends on a verification result. With the dial set to autonomous, no gate waits for the sign-off sheet, which lists the declarations, the claims the system added, the claims stated as hypotheses, the decisions a third family made and the skipped steps.

We built galley's behaviours one at a time. We wrote a behaviour, showed it working, and only then built the next, until the chain of working behaviours covered the full ladder.

## Failures and outages

The split between required behaviours and improvers decides how galley responds when a step fails. When an improver fails twice, galley skips it and records the effect. If the skipped improver leaves a claim without evidence, galley hedges the claim. Galley omits a figure when the improver that draws it fails twice. A skipped improver can change what the manuscript asserts and contains, but not whether it exists.

Galley limits how long it waits when a provider hits a usage limit or the search index becomes unavailable. When a model provider hits a usage limit, galley waits it out for up to about six hours without counting a failure; a longer limit pauses the run until it is resumed. When the search index is unavailable, galley waits for up to three hours. If the index remains unavailable after that wait, galley hedges the affected claims and manuscript production continues.

## Seats across model families

Galley assigns work to seats and assigns the seats to model families. The seats are author, checker, challenger, verifier, referee and adjudicator. In this run, Claude Opus 5.5 was the author, GPT-6.2 Sol the checker, and Gemini 4 Carbon the challenger and verifier.

Galley separates families through rules on specific role pairs. The checker proposes each citation, and the verifier, from another family, judges it. Referee seats go to families other than the author's and rotate between rounds. The referee who raised a finding judges the author's answer to it. Adjudication goes to the family that is neither the author's nor the referee's. The family that proposes new directions for the seed does not choose among them. After review, a family other than the author's reads the final text against every claim in the ledger. Galley does not track contribution provenance across all review assignments, so the separation holds for these pairs only. Outside them, a family can review work it contributed to: in this run, a referee seat from the GPT family could review citations that GPT-6.2 Sol proposed as checker.

## Challenging the seed and rescoring the paper

Galley challenges the seed before writing any part of the manuscript. The `review-idea` behaviour scores the idea on seven impact factors, names the weakest and gives a verdict: worth writing, reformulate, or no contribution. When the idea should be reframed, `reformulate` proposes three structurally different directions that preserve the seed's explicit commitments. In `select-direction`, a model family other than the proposer then selects the original idea or one of the three directions. If one of these improvers fails twice, galley skips it and continues manuscript production.

After review, `reprofile` scores the finished manuscript again. Both sets of scores are heuristic self-assessments made by models inside the run. They are not predictions of impact, and we do not treat them as evidence that this or any paper will have impact. Section 8 returns to this limit.
editorBase.S5:
This section describes the path a claim takes from the search for its evidence to its standing in the claim ledger.  Verification and reconciliation can change the claim's scope. Verification sets a claim's standing as supported, narrowed, or hypothesis. Drafting instructions direct `draft` to match that standing, and reconciliation can later confirm, narrow, or drop the ledger entry.  

## Retrieval through Canary

The plan marks each claim as needing external evidence, as the authors' own work, or as a premise. Evidence search covers only the first kind. The labels are model judgments that no behaviour is assigned to check. A seed claim that needs outside support but is labelled otherwise skips search and verification, is stated as fact and does not reach the sign-off sheet, though a referee can still raise it. Claims of these two kinds that `plan` adds go to the sign-off sheet as claims the system added.  For each claim that needs evidence, `find-evidence` writes literature searches and runs them through Canary, the authors' search tool over the OpenAlex scholarly catalogue. From the abstracts the searches return, it selects up to ten candidate passages, each copied verbatim.

Retrieval stays in Canary by design. Galley writes the queries and reads the abstracts that Canary returns. This division keeps galley to one task, manuscript production, and leaves retrieval to a separate tool.

## Verbatim passages and registry records

Code, not a model, establishes where every cited passage comes from and, for works with a DOI, where the bibliographic record comes from. Before citation, code checks that the passage reproduces text from the cited work's abstract verbatim. The draft cannot cite a passage that fails this check. When the cited work has a DOI, its bibliographic record comes from the DOI registry and not from model output. A citation therefore cannot rest on an invented passage, and a cited work with a DOI cannot carry an invented bibliographic record. The registry check does not cover cited works without a DOI.

This check settles provenance, not relevance. A verbatim passage from a real work can still fail to support the claim it is attached to. Judging that fit is the verifier's task. Because every passage comes from an abstract, verification judges claims against abstracts and not against full texts. 

## Cross-family verdicts

The checker and verifier come from different model families. The checker proposes a candidate passage. The verifier, from a different family, judges it against its claim and returns one of three verdicts. A verdict of *supported* means the passage supports the claim, and the citation stands. When the verdict is *narrower*, galley narrows the claim to what the passage states. When the verdict is *not supported*, galley rejects the citation and tries the next candidate passage.

Narrowing reduces what a claim asserts until it matches a verified passage.  When the verifier rejects every candidate for a claim, the claim ends without verified evidence and takes hypothesis standing. Galley lists the claim on the sign-off sheet and instructs `draft` to state it as a hypothesis. A *not supported* verdict covers passages that are silent on a claim and passages that contradict it, so hypothesis standing does not show which of the two the verifier found. 

The split between checker and verifier is one of the role-pair separation rules in Section 4: the family that proposes a candidate passage does not act as verifier for that passage. This run does not show whether cross-family verification catches more defects than same-family verification. 

## Drafting and fidelity

At drafting, code enforces citation selection while instructions govern how prose reflects claim standing. The `draft` behaviour writes each section from its claims, their standings, and any verified passages. Code restricts `draft` to citing only passages that passed verification. Drafting instructions direct `draft` to keep each claim within its standing and to state any claim with hypothesis standing as a hypothesis rather than as established fact. Code does not check whether the drafted prose follows those instructions. 

Post-draft checking reviews sentence scope through model judgment rather than code enforcement. A drafted sentence can still say more than its claim or evidence. The `fidelity` improver checks each drafted section and rewrites sentences that exceed their claim's standing or verified passage, but it can miss overclaims. Claims marked as the authors' own work or as premises carry no passage, so `fidelity` checks their sentences against the planned claim alone. If `fidelity` fails twice, galley skips it and lists the skipped check on the sign-off sheet for author review.

## Calibration of the verifier

Galley tests the verifier against planted defects on each run, and the production record reports only the resulting catch count. The `calibrate` behaviour plants defective citations among the verified ones, mixes in unaltered controls, and measures how many of the planted defects the verifier catches. The production record omits the number of controls and the verdicts on them. The specification of galley's mechanics generated for this manuscript also omits how `calibrate` constructs planted defects and which outcomes count as a catch.

The reported count measures sensitivity to a run's planted defects, not specificity or verifier reliability. A verifier that rejected every candidate would also catch every planted defect, and without control outcomes the verifier's false-rejection rate remains unknown. The count also covers only one verifier on the claims of one run, not other seeds or fields. This run does not show whether the count predicts how often the verifier catches citation errors outside the planted set.

## Reconciling the ledger with the text

The `reconcile` improver runs only after review to align the claim ledger with the final text, and its outcome rests on model judgment. Drafting and revisions during review can narrow or change the prose while the ledger still holds earlier wording. Referees therefore read an unreconciled ledger and do not check `reconcile` verdicts. Once review finishes, a family other than the author's reads the final text against every claim in the ledger. For each claim, it confirms the ledger entry, narrows the entry to the text's wording, or drops it as no longer stated. The claim ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet then reflect those verdicts rather than a code-verified match with the prose. If `reconcile` fails twice, galley skips it, names the skipped step on the sign-off sheet and leaves unaligned ledger entries in place until the authors sign off.

Each reconcile verdict can be audited. Galley stores every prompt and answer, including each verdict, in the paper's folder alongside the production journal, and a rerun replays them without calling a model. The manuscript ends with the claim ledger, which gives each claim's standing and sources, and with a production record generated from the same journal. A reader can trace each confirmed or narrowed claim from its ledger entry to the verdict that set its standing. The trace for a dropped claim starts from the stored reconcile verdict that dropped it.
editorBase.S6:
The referee seats read the draft manuscript and raise findings. The author answers each material finding. A third model family adjudicates any material finding that remains disputed at the answer cap. This section describes that loop, the optional controls through which a person can take part, and the package that each run writes.

## Cross-family referee seats

Four referee seats review the manuscript: methods, the host field, citations and the desk editor. Each seat is drawn from a model family other than the author's, and the seats rotate between those families from one round to the next. Every seat reads the whole manuscript. Each seat specifies a severity and a requested decision for every finding it raises.

## The capped answer-and-judge loop

The author answers each material finding in one of four forms. The author can fix the finding and give the exact edits. The author can also rebut the finding, state it as a limitation, or mark it as needing evidence. A finding that needs evidence prompts a new claim. That claim goes through search and verification.

The referee who raised a finding judges the author's answer. In this run, the cap was three author answers per finding. A finding still disputed at the cap goes to adjudication. A third model family settles the finding. Each decision made this way also appears on the sign-off sheet described below.

Each family uses its own command-line client without tools and returns answers that conform to a strict JSON schema. Galley stores every prompt and answer. A rerun replays the stored answers without calling a model. The same store gives people the full provenance of each finding, answer, judgement and adjudication.

## Optional human participation

Galley offers optional controls for human participation. They can edit the document directly or comment anywhere in it. A direct edit becomes that person's revision on the next run.

Each comment becomes a thread with one of three ownership settings. By default the agents take it over. The person keeps a thread marked `@humans`. The person and the agents share a thread marked `@both`. In a shared thread, the agents' changes arrive as proposed edits placed in the document. This follows the side-chat pattern of poise, the authors' editor. The person accepts or declines each proposed edit and stays in charge of the text.

Citation selection is automatic by default. With citation choices turned on, each claim waits for the person. The person chooses among the claim's candidate sources (a, b, c), lets the system pick, or states the claim without a source. Each candidate is a passage that code confirms is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract. Whoever picks it, the verifier, a family other than the checker's, judges the passage against the claim and can narrow the claim to what the passage states. A claim stated without a source has no verified evidence, so the draft states it as a hypothesis and the sign-off sheet lists it. On every path, the claim ledger records the claim's standing and origin.

The dial controls which steps wait for a person. It can make load-bearing citations and critical answers wait, or it can make every answer wait.

## The manuscript package

Galley 0.1.0 is open source under the MIT licence, with source at https://github.com/autonomio/galley. From a text seed alone, it produces a complete manuscript package: a PDF, a line-numbered review PDF, LaTeX, Word, the editor document, an evidence package and a sign-off sheet. It also writes a production journal for each run.

Each manuscript ends with its claim ledger and a production record. The claim ledger lists every claim with its kind, its standing, its origin in the seed or the system, and its sources. Galley generates the production record from the run's journal.

Each paper also gets its own evidence package in the Resolvent format, which the run writes as part of the manuscript package. The package holds the reconciled claims, the bibliographic record of each cited work, and the verbatim abstract passage behind each citation, which galley finds through Canary's search over OpenAlex. Typesetting renders each citation key as a reference-list entry from the cited work's bibliographic record; when the work has a DOI, that record and its DOI come from the DOI registry. From the manuscript alone, a reader can use a citation key to find its reference entry and every claim-ledger entry that lists the cited work among its sources (Appendix A). When one work supports several claims, the reader identifies the relevant ledger entry from the wording of the citing sentence, then looks up the cited work externally to read the claim against its abstract. The evidence package adds the accepted passage itself, paired with its claim and record.

The sign-off sheet lists what only the authors can decide: declarations, claims the system added, claims stated as hypotheses, decisions a third family made, and skipped steps.

Together, the claim ledger, the evidence package, the production record and the sign-off sheet state what the manuscript claims and on what evidence. They also record how the run reached the text and what the authors still have to decide.
editorBase.S7:
## Run and method

This manuscript is galley's first production. Galley compiled it from the authors' seed in one autonomous run, set for two referee rounds and a preprint venue.   Galley generated a specification of its mechanics from its code, seats and package metadata. The models drafted the sections that describe galley from that specification.

We evaluate scope-elastic compilation in an instrumented case study of this run; the same run wrote the case study. From the run's production record we report how many claims ended narrowed or stated as hypotheses, how many planted defects the verifier caught, and how the run resolved referee findings. The claim ledger at the end of the manuscript gives the kind and standing of every claim it keeps, including claims that ended supported.

No model supplied any of these numbers. Code generates the record from the run's journal and fills it in each time the text is typeset, so the table states the run at the revision it accompanies. Each typeset writes the PDF, a line-numbered review PDF, LaTeX, Word, the editor document, the evidence package in the Resolvent format and the sign-off sheet. The paper's folder also keeps the production journal and every prompt and answer.    

## Production record
